claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 in the target state has a hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations and complex microelastic fields.
A signal-processing-enhanced RUS and physics-informed reduced-order model can rapidly and accurately predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
RUS can provide macroscopic elastic-modulus measurements for a refractory high-entropy alloy that agree with theoretical calculations.
Advanced filtering of RUS measurements can extract effective local elastic fields.
RUS-derived local elastic-field descriptors capture the effects of multilevel chemical fluctuations on the microelastic response of HfNbTiVAl10.
Established elasticity scaling laws can map localized RUS-derived elastic fields to bulk mechanical properties.
Sparse Bayesian calibration can refine the mapping from RUS descriptors to the target mechanical properties.
Yield strength can be predicted from measured elastic moduli using the proposed calibrated mapping.
Fracture toughness can be predicted from measured elastic moduli using the proposed calibrated mapping.
The proposed method will reduce computational time by approximately three to four orders of magnitude relative to full-scale CALPHAD and first-principles methods.
The proposed method will improve predictive accuracy for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness by 10–20%.
The method is applicable at room and elevated temperatures under tensile and controlled-fracture test conditions.
The method remains reliable when the microstructural fluctuations and defect distributions lie within the model’s calibration range.
Excessive RUS signal noise can cause the method to fail.
Extreme microsegregation, unforeseen defects, or new microstructural phenomena outside the calibration range can cause the method to fail.

Full CALPHAD, first-principles, and conventional machine-learning approaches require extensive computational resources and are inefficient for predicting fracture toughness in hierarchical heterostructures.
In single-phase BCC NbTaTiV, RUS-derived elastic moduli agree well with in situ neutron-diffraction, first-principles, and machine-learning results.
